newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia-Europe try to chart future course.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Europe try to chart future course.

text.p: Foreign ministers from 25 countries met on Saturday to chart the future of ties between Asia and Europe, with the problem of Burma hovering over the discussions.
Talks focused on how to discuss sensitive political issues, ways to boost economic and cultural ties and whether to allow new members to join the Asia-Europe meetings (ASEM), delegates said.
But they said no great initiatives were likely to come out of the meeting.
"It's a useful exercise," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring told reporters before the meeting: "But we don't expect it to generate anything."

Burma, whose suppression of a pro-democracy movement led by Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi has been denounced by European nations, could be discussed, due to its imminent membership in ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations).
"Should an ASEAN member be given automatic membership in ASEM? It's a delicate situation principally because of Myanmar (Burma)," one Asian diplomat said.
Burma is due to join ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- possibly as early as this year.
Japan, China and South Korea join the ASEAN countries on the Asian side for these talks with the 15-member European Union to prepare for a second ASEM summit due to be held in London next April.
An inaugural ASEM summit in Bangkok last year agreed Europe would manage European membership of the group and Asia would handle Asian participation.

The Asian side is debating giving ASEM membership to Australia, New Zealand, India and Pakistan, but has not agreed on whether all should come in. Some European countries have proposed membership for Russia.
Burma, whose top officials are banned from Europe, could be a serious problem unless a solution is found before the London summit.
Saturday's meeting was expected to debate how to tackle political and human rights issues and Asia's belief that ASEM should focus on economic ties.
"The feeling among the Asians is that ASEM should give primacy to economic issues. If we let political issues dominate, this will just be like the United Nations," one Asian diplomat said.
The diplomat said that compared to the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, ASEM gets bogged down in tackling non-economic issues.
"The Europeans don't like talk of trade liberalisation. There's an inclination to drag their feet on this issue," an Asian official said.
Delegates said ASEM completed the third leg of a global strategic triangle, after the trans-Pacific APEC grouping and the Trans-Atlantic meeting between North America and Europe.
"The weak link in this triangular relationship was between Asia and Europe," Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar told a welcoming dinner.
"ASEM must strengthen the political dialogue between the two regions on the basis of equality and mutual respect," he said.
European delegates say a political dimension is important to the talks.
"The Asians want to have the economic cooperation and the technology transfer without all the lectures," one European delegate said.
